main_text.p: Lorinusp interpret the first de compositi totius dissolutione, of the dissolution of the parts of the whole man, consisting of body and soul; the second of the state of the soul separated from the body; and the third of the disposing of the body parted from the soul. Thus the Scriptures' speech of being gathered to our people should be answerable in meaning to the phrase used by the heathen of descending into hell or going to Hades: which, as Synesiusq noteth out of Homer, was by them opposed τῇ ἀκριβεστάτῃ ἀπωλείᾳ, to a most absolute extinguishment as well of the soul as of the body. And forasmuch as by that term, the immortality of the soul was commonly signified: therefore doth Plato in his Phædo disputing of that argument, make this the state of his question: "Whetherr the souls of men deceased be in Hades or no?" and Olympiodorus, the Alexandrian deacon, affirmeth of Job, that he delivered "thes most excellent doctrine of the immortality of the soul;" by teaching, "that souls are not extinguished together with their bodies, but do remain in Hades;" and some others also of our ecclesiastical writers do from thence fetch a difference between death and Hades. "Yout shall find," said Theophylact, "that there is some difference between Hades and death: namely that Hades containeth the souls, but death the bodies. For the souls are immortal."
